## Lab 8 - Danielle Goedhart

```{r}
library(parallel)
library(microbenchmark)
```

**Vectorization**

1\.

```{r}
fun1 <- function(n = 100, k = 4, lambda = 4) {
  x <- NULL
  
  for (i in 1:n){
    x <- rbind(x, rpois(k, lambda))    
  }
  
  return(x)
}

fun1alt <- function(n = 100, k = 4, lambda = 4) {
  matrix(
    rpois(n * k, lambda),
    nrow = n,
    ncol = k,
    byrow = TRUE
  )
}

# Check that they have the same dimensions
dim(fun1())
dim(fun1alt())

# Check that they have similar distributions
summary(fun1())
summary(fun1alt())

mean(fun1())
mean(fun1alt())

# Compare their speeds
microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  fun1(),
  fun1alt()
)
```

Both fun1() and fun1alt() generate matrices with 100 rows and 4 columns. The values follow similar distributions, with overall means of 3.965 and 4.045, respectively. Both of these means are close to the specified Poisson mean of 4. Based on the microbenchmark results, fun1alt() is faster than fun1(), with an average execution time of 94 and 1228 microseconds, respectively.

2\.

```{r}
# Data Generating Process (10 x 10,000 matrix)
set.seed(1234)
x <- matrix(rnorm(1e4), nrow = 10)

# Find each column's max value
fun2 <- function(x) {
  apply(x, 2, max)
}

fun2alt <- function(x) {
  do.call(pmax, unname(split(x, row(x))))
}

# Show that both functions return the same output
head(fun2(x), 10)
head(fun2alt(x), 10)

identical(fun2(x), fun2alt(x))

# Compare their speeds
microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  fun2(x),
  fun2alt(x)
)
```

Both fun2() and fun2alt() returned the same output for the given matrix, all the values match, and it returns TRUE. Fun2alt() was faster than fun2(), with an average execution time of 702 versus 2145 microseconds, respectively.

**Parallelization**

1\.

```{r}
my_boot <- function(dat, stat, R, ncpus = 1L) {
  
  # Getting the random indices
  n <- nrow(dat)
  idx <- matrix(sample.int(n, n * R, TRUE), nrow = n, ncol = R)
  
  # Create a cluster using the number of cores in ncpus
  cl <- makeCluster(ncpus)
  
  # Stop the cluster when the function finishes
  on.exit(stopCluster(cl))
  
  # Parallelized version of lapply
  ans <- parLapply(
    cl,
    seq_len(R),
    function(i, dat, idx, stat) {
      stat(dat[idx[, i], , drop = FALSE])
    },
    dat = dat,
    idx = idx,
    stat = stat
  )
  
  # Converting the list into a matrix
  ans <- do.call(rbind, ans)
  
  return(ans)
}
```

2\.

```{r}
# Bootstrap of an OLS
my_stat <- function(d) coef(lm(y ~ x, data=d))

# DATA SIM
set.seed(1)
n <- 500; R <- 1e4

x <- cbind(rnorm(n)); y <- x*5 + rnorm(n)

# Checking if we get something similar as lm
ans0 <- confint(lm(y~x))
ans1 <- my_boot(dat = data.frame(x, y), my_stat, R = R, ncpus = 2L)

# You should get something like this
t(apply(ans1, 2, quantile, c(.025,.975)))
##                   2.5%      97.5%
## (Intercept) -0.1372435 0.05074397
## x            4.8680977 5.04539763
ans0
##                  2.5 %     97.5 %
## (Intercept) -0.1379033 0.04797344
## x            4.8650100 5.04883353
```

The bootstrap confidence intervals are very similar to the confidence intervals from the linear model, showing that the parallel bootstrap function provides accurate results.

3\.

```{r}
system.time(my_boot(dat = data.frame(x, y), my_stat, R = 4000, ncpus = 1L))
system.time(my_boot(dat = data.frame(x, y), my_stat, R = 4000, ncpus = 2L))
```

The version using two cores was faster than the version using one core.
